title: Fuel a Future:
format: 16:9 only · 1920×1080 (event film, plays in the room)
headline: Every community in the world has business, and most schools still don't teach it. NFTE and BUILD are joining forces to change that, and it has to happen now.
story: An event film for a global audience. Open on the missing subject: reading, writing, arithmetic, and entrepreneurship. J.D. makes the case: every community has business, all schools should teach it, and schools around the world have missed it. In a world of AI, students need their creative capabilities, the skills of teams, problems, opportunities and the future. That is an optimistic moment, and it creates mobility and jobs.

The turn is the merger, said out loud. J.D.: NFTE is taking it a step further, merging and partnering with others. Then the word the client asked for: one line from the merger video that says BUILD. Then urgency: Right now we need to be doing more. The button lands on entrepreneurship as a core subject, over the celebration, and the end card says Fuel a Future with both logos.
Loops: L1 What subject is school missing? opens at 0:00, closes at 00:26 (the gap). L2 Who fixes it, and why now? opens at the turn (01:09), closes on the button. Hopeful and urgent, never fearful.
do: Open on the classroom shot with the hook text on screen at frame 1.
Lower third on J.D.'s first on-camera line only (00:17).
Say BUILD: J.D.'s merger line, then one line from the merger video with the word BUILD.
Show BUILD students in at least two shots (row 01:09).
End card: Fuel a Future, the NFTE and BUILD logos, nfte.com/fuelafuture. Hold it to the last frame.
dont: No city, state or country name on screen. No slide, sign or backdrop text that names a place.
No US-only phrasing in captions except the U.S. schooling line, which he widens himself.
Do not write the word merger on screen: J.D. says merging and partnering.
No logos or history at the top. No black frames, no fade from or to black.
No BUILD shot with their name bars, circle graphics, logos or subtitles burned in.

Times are mm:ss.s in each file. Speaker labels were wrong and are removed: every answer is J.D.; lines that start with Q: are the interviewer. The machine wrote "Nifty"; it is written NFTE here, as he says it. The pitch-competition file has line times only (no word times).

[00:06.0] Q: What's something you've changed your mind about in education?
[00:11.8] One thing I've changed my mind about in education is the extent to which the balance of effort should be spent on skill development as opposed to content knowledge.
[00:23.5] I think it used to be the case in education that it was very very important to really know a lot of facts and figures and operations.
[00:35.3] It's still somewhat important to know those things.
[00:38.6] But the fact is technology and automation, but also the way in which the world and the world of work are changing really puts the emphasis these days on the importance of developing higher order skills in young people and in learners.
[00:57.7] So, when I think about the types of things that I wish I had spent more time cultivating as a student myself, it's many of the things that we at NFTE speak about as the entrepreneurial mindset.
[01:12.6] The ability to work in teams, the ability to solve problems, the ability to spot opportunities, the ability to think about the future.
[01:22.6] These are not things that traditional school necessarily focuses on, even though when you stop and think about it, they're not only crucial for entrepreneurship, they're really crucial for just getting along in life day to day.
[01:39.3] The most fundamental thing that I think about these days when it comes to education is that it's really important to develop a sense of agency and positivity and self-motivation and self-confidence.
[02:01.2] Education systems have always tried to speak broadly to that, but I don't think they've ever really tried to organize what they do to truly cultivate it, and I think that's what's needed in education.
[02:15.7] I think it's needed in a major way and really the balance of effort of schooling ought to transformatively shift in this direction, in my opinion.

[00:04.4] Q: How does NFTE reflect where education is heading, not just where it's been?
[00:10.8] NFTE reflects where education is heading because NFTE is about entrepreneurship.
[00:18.3] Entrepreneurship is fundamentally about creation.
[00:22.3] Education needs sorely now to head in the direction of cultivating students' creative capabilities in a world of artificial intelligence, in a world of changing professions and changing industries, in a world where the traditional methods are not producing the academic achievement results that students need, and we all can see it, the world and students most of all need something different.
[00:51.2] NFTE's here not just to spread the gospel of entrepreneurship education, we are now here to reinvent education for what it needs to be, but frankly, what it always should have been.
[01:04.6] And that's what NFTE is about.
[01:07.0] Q: And what does learning by doing unlock for students?
[01:12.3] Learning by doing, first of all, unlocks the fact that students want to do things.
[01:19.8] People want to do things.
[01:22.2] Young people do not want to sit all the time in a classroom and hear about theoretical, conceptual things.
[01:32.2] They want to have a purpose in the world.
[01:35.4] They want to find out who they're about.
[01:38.8] And learning by doing allows young people to do those things.
[01:43.0] Sol Helendie.
[01:44.2] Q: As NFTE approaches its 40th anniversary in 2027, how do these ideas reflect the organization's enduring relevance, and what do they say about NFTE's role in shaping the future of education?
[01:59.5] NFTE's enduring relevance over 40 years comes from the fact that the world is full of businesses.
[02:05.8] You can't have a world without them.
[02:07.4] You can't have an economy without them.
